---
title: Tensor-Product Chebyshev Tables
---

A smooth scalar function of several variables that is expensive to evaluate can be
tabulated once and recomputed from the table. The table described on this page divides the
domain of the function into panels and stores, for each panel, the coefficients of a
tensor product of Chebyshev series. The value of the function at a point is approximated
by the sum of the series of the panel that contains the point. The table is efficient for
a smooth function, because its Chebyshev series converge quickly and each panel then
stores few coefficients. The class [[numcosmo-math|NcmSpectralTensor]] is the table. The
class [[numcosmo-math|NcmSpectralTensorBuilder]] computes the table from the function,
with an estimated error below a requested tolerance.

The caller sets the domain of the table, one interval per variable, and may split it at
chosen values of a variable, for example where the function has a kink. The builder then
expands the function on each subdomain that is not yet filled. It evaluates the function
on Chebyshev--Lobatto grids and estimates the error of the series from its coefficients of
highest order. When the estimate is below the tolerance, the series is stored as a panel.
Otherwise the builder adds points along one variable, or bisects the subdomain along it,
and repeats.

```{python}
#| echo: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle
from numcosmo_py import Ncm

Ncm.cfg_init()
```

## The Domain and its Tree

The table approximates a real function $F (x_0, \dots, x_{n - 1})$ of $n$ variables,
$1 \le n \le 16$, on the domain
$$
\Omega \equiv [a_0, b_0] \times [a_1, b_1] \times \dots \times [a_{n - 1}, b_{n - 1}] ,
\tag{1}
$$
where $a_i < b_i$ are the ends of the range of variable $i$. The table divides $\Omega$
recursively, and the subdomains form a tree. Each node of the tree has a subdomain, the
Cartesian product of one interval per variable. The interval of a node in variable $i$
is $[p_i, q_i]$. The subdomain of the root is $\Omega$, so for the root $p_i = a_i$ and
$q_i = b_i$. A node is of one of three kinds, and only a split node has children.

- A split node divides its subdomain along one variable $i$. It has the interior edges
  $p_i < e_1 < \dots < e_{m - 1} < q_i$, with $m \ge 2$, and $m$ children. The intervals
  of the children in variable $i$ are $[p_i, e_1], [e_1, e_2], \dots, [e_{m - 1}, q_i]$.
  In the other variables, the intervals of the children are those of the node.
- A panel node is not divided and holds a series
  ([The Series on a Panel](#the-series-on-a-panel)).
- An empty node is not divided and holds no series. It becomes a split node or a panel
  node when the table is filled.

The children of a split node cover its subdomain, and two children intersect only on the
face at their common edge. The panels of a table with no empty node therefore cover
$\Omega$ and intersect only on their boundaries. The bounds $p_i$, $q_i$ of a node follow
from Eq. (1) and from the split nodes between the root and the node. The caller does not
give them.

Nodes are numbered in the order they are created, and the root is node 0. The children of
a split node have consecutive numbers. A panel node also has a panel number, from 0, in
the order the series are set. A table is filled by four operations.

- The domain $\Omega$ is set, and the root becomes an empty node. The function
  [[numcosmo-math|ncm_spectral_tensor_set_domain]] implements this operation.
- An empty node becomes a split node, given the variable and the interior edges. The
  function [[numcosmo-math|ncm_spectral_tensor_split]] implements this operation.
- Every empty node is split along one variable, at the edges of a given list that are
  strictly inside the interval of the node in that variable. One such operation per
  variable divides $\Omega$ into a grid. The function
  [[numcosmo-math|ncm_spectral_tensor_split_empty]] implements this operation.
- An empty node becomes a panel node, given the coefficients of its series. The function
  [[numcosmo-math|ncm_spectral_tensor_set_panel]] implements this operation.

A table of two variables divided by these operations is shown in @fig-tree.

```{python}
#| label: fig-tree
#| fig-cap: >
#|   A table on $[0, 1]^2$ filled by the four operations, without the builder. The
#|   domain is divided into a grid at $x_0 = 0.5$ and $x_1 = 0.5$. The subdomain that
#|   contains the point $(0.30, 0.14)$, drawn as a dot, is then bisected six times, in
#|   $x_0$ and in $x_1$ alternately, each time on the half that contains the point. The
#|   table has 19 nodes: 9 split nodes and 10 panel nodes. Each rectangle is a panel,
#|   labeled with its panel number and colored by the number of split nodes between the
#|   root and its panel node, from 2 to 8. The outlined panel is the one that
#|   `ncm_spectral_tensor_find_panel` returns for the point.
#| code-fold: true
EMPTY = Ncm.SpectralTensorNodeKind.EMPTY
SPLIT = Ncm.SpectralTensorNodeKind.SPLIT

point = np.array([0.30, 0.14])
st = Ncm.SpectralTensor.new(2)
st.set_domain([0.0, 0.0], [1.0, 1.0])
st.split_empty(0, [0.5])
st.split_empty(1, [0.5])



def holds_point(k):
    """Whether the subdomain of node k holds the point."""
    lower, upper = st.get_node_bounds(k)
    return all(lo <= x < up for lo, x, up in zip(lower, point, upper))


# The empty node that holds the point, bisected six times toward it.
node = next(
    k
    for k in range(st.get_n_nodes())
    if st.get_node_kind(k) == EMPTY and holds_point(k)
)
for step in range(6):
    lower, upper = st.get_node_bounds(node)
    i = step % 2
    mid = 0.5 * (lower[i] + upper[i])
    node = st.split(node, i, [mid]) + (1 if point[i] >= mid else 0)

# Every empty node becomes a panel node with one coefficient.
for k in range(st.get_n_nodes()):
    if st.get_node_kind(k) == EMPTY:
        st.set_panel(k, [1, 1], [1.0])

# The number of split nodes above each node; a child has a larger number than its parent.
depth = np.zeros(st.get_n_nodes(), dtype=int)
n_splits = 0
for k in range(st.get_n_nodes()):
    if st.get_node_kind(k) == SPLIT:
        edges, _, first_child = st.get_node_split(k)
        depth[first_child : first_child + len(edges) + 1] = depth[k] + 1
        n_splits += 1

assert (st.get_n_nodes(), n_splits, st.get_n_panels(), st.get_n_empty()) == (19, 9, 10, 0)

found = st.find_panel(point)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 6.0))
cmap = plt.get_cmap("viridis_r")
for k in range(st.get_n_nodes()):
    if st.get_node_kind(k) in (EMPTY, SPLIT):
        continue
    p = st.get_node_panel(k)
    lower, upper = st.get_node_bounds(k)
    width, height = upper[0] - lower[0], upper[1] - lower[1]
    ax.add_patch(
        Rectangle(
            (lower[0], lower[1]),
            width,
            height,
            facecolor=cmap((depth[k] - 2) / 6.0),
            edgecolor="red" if p == found else "black",
            linewidth=2.5 if p == found else 0.8,
            zorder=3 if p == found else 2,
        )
    )
    if min(width, height) > 0.05:
        ax.text(
            lower[0] + 0.5 * width,
            lower[1] + 0.5 * height,
            str(p),
            ha="center",
            va="center",
            color="white" if depth[k] > 4 else "black",
        )
ax.plot(*point, "o", color="red", markersize=4, zorder=4)
ax.set_xlim(0.0, 1.0)
ax.set_ylim(0.0, 1.0)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.set_xlabel("$x_0$")
ax.set_ylabel("$x_1$")
plt.show()
```

## The Series on a Panel

A panel is the subdomain of a panel node,
$$
\mathcal{P} \equiv [p_0, q_0] \times [p_1, q_1] \times \dots \times [p_{n - 1}, q_{n - 1}] ,
\tag{2}
$$
where $[p_i, q_i]$ is the interval of the panel node in variable $i$, together with the
series that approximates $F$ on it. On $\mathcal{P}$ the table approximates $F$ by
$$
F (x_0, \dots, x_{n - 1}) \approx \sum_{k_0 = 0}^{K_0 - 1} \dots \sum_{k_{n - 1} = 0}^{K_{n - 1} - 1} c^{k_0 \dots k_{n - 1}} \prod_{i = 0}^{n - 1} T_{k_i} (s_i) ,
\qquad
s_i \equiv \frac{2 x_i - p_i - q_i}{q_i - p_i} ,
\tag{3}
$$
where $T_k$ is the Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind and degree $k$,
$s_i \in [-1, 1]$ is the Chebyshev variable of $x_i$ on the panel, $K_i \ge 1$ is the
number of coefficients of the panel in variable $i$, and $c^{k_0 \dots k_{n - 1}}$ are the
coefficients of the panel. The numbers $K_i$ may differ between variables and between
panels. For $n = 1$, Eq. (3) reduces to Eq. (1) of
[Spectral Methods](spectral.qmd#chebyshev-representation), with $N = K_0$.

The coefficients of a panel are stored with the first variable running fastest: the
coefficient $c^{k_0 \dots k_{n - 1}}$ is at position $k_0 + K_0 (k_1 + K_1 (k_2 + \dots))$.

## Evaluation

The table is evaluated at a point $(x_0, \dots, x_{n - 1})$ in two steps. The function
[[numcosmo-math|ncm_spectral_tensor_eval]] implements both.

1. The tree is searched for the panel that contains the point. The search starts at the
   root. At a split node of variable $i$ with interior edges $e_1 < \dots < e_{m - 1}$,
   the interior edges at or below $x_i$ are counted by bisection. The count, from 0 to
   $m - 1$, is the position of a child among the $m$ children of the split node, and the
   search continues at that child. The search ends at a panel node. The function
   [[numcosmo-math|ncm_spectral_tensor_find_panel]] implements this search.
2. The series of the panel, Eq. (3), is summed. With two to four variables, the values
   $T_k (s_i)$, $k < K_i$, are computed first for each variable. Up to 33 values are
   computed in few dependent steps: for the first variable by the product formulas
   $T_{2 k} = 2 T_k^2 - 1$ and $T_{2 k + 1} = 2 T_k T_{k + 1} - s$, and for the other
   variables in four chains $T_{k + 4} = 2 T_4 T_k - T_{k - 4}$. More than 33 values are
   computed by the recurrence $T_{k + 1} = 2 s T_k - T_{k - 1}$, whose error near
   $s = \pm 1$ is the smallest of the three: the errors are equal up to 17 values, and
   those of the other two are twice as large at 33. The sum over $k_0$,
   $u^{k_1 \dots k_{n - 1}} \equiv \sum_{k_0} c^{k_0 \dots k_{n - 1}} T_{k_0} (s_0)$, is
   then the dot product of one row of coefficients with the values $T_{k_0} (s_0)$, and
   four rows are summed in one pass. A row of up to 33 coefficients is summed by code
   compiled for its length. The sums over $k_1, \dots, k_{n - 1}$ weight these values
   with $T_{k_i} (s_i)$. The dot products do not depend on each other, so the processor
   computes several at once, while each step of a Clenshaw recurrence depends on the step
   before. With one variable the series is summed by a Clenshaw recurrence, which is
   faster for one series of up to about 100 coefficients. With five variables or more, or
   with more than 1025 coefficients in one variable, the series is summed by Clenshaw
   recurrences nested from $s_{n - 1}$ to $s_0$. In every case the sum takes
   $\prod_i K_i$ multiplications by coefficients. The function
   [[numcosmo-math|ncm_spectral_tensor_eval_on]] implements this sum.

By the rule of step 1, a point on an interior edge belongs to the child whose interval
starts at that edge. The search does not check that the point is in $\Omega$. A
coordinate below every interior edge of a split node leads to the first child, and a
coordinate at or above every interior edge leads to the last child. A point outside
$\Omega$ therefore reaches the panel that contains the point of $\Omega$ obtained by
clamping each coordinate $x_i$ to $[a_i, b_i]$, and the series of that panel is
extrapolated. The tolerance of the table does not apply to an extrapolated value, and the
evaluation does not report it. A point that may be outside $\Omega$ is therefore compared
with the intervals $[a_i, b_i]$ before the evaluation, and the function is computed
directly at a point outside. The ends $a_i$ and $b_i$ are read with
[[numcosmo-math|ncm_spectral_tensor_get_range]]. A search that reaches an empty node
aborts with an error.

For several points of one panel, the panel is found once, and its series is summed at
each point with [[numcosmo-math|ncm_spectral_tensor_eval_on]]. The search and
the sum do not change the table, so one table may be evaluated in several threads at
once.

Several points can also be evaluated in one operation. The panel of each point is found
as in step 1, and consecutive points on the same panel are summed together, 8 points at a
time. With two to four variables, the values $T_k (s_i)$ of the 8 points are computed by
the recurrence $T_{k + 1} (s) = 2 s T_k (s) - T_{k - 1} (s)$, and each coefficient is then
multiplied into the 8 points at once. With one variable, the 8 points are summed by 8
Clenshaw recurrences. Every sum over an index runs from the last index to the first, so
the terms of a decaying series are added from the smallest, and the rounding error is that
of the Clenshaw recurrences. The values agree with those of the evaluation of one point
to rounding, not bit by bit. Points ordered along a line, or grouped by panel, form the
longest runs of points on one panel. A panel with more than 129 coefficients in one
variable, and any panel of a table of five variables or more, is summed point by point as
in step 2. The function [[numcosmo-math|ncm_spectral_tensor_eval_array]] implements this
operation.

## Expansion on a Node

The table is built by expanding $F$ on each empty node, in the order of the node numbers.
The domain must be set before the construction, and nodes may be split beforehand, for
example at a kink of $F$. A node whose series does not reach the tolerance is split
further ([Refinement](#refinement)). The function
[[numcosmo-math|ncm_spectral_tensor_builder_build]] implements this construction.

On a node with the subdomain of Eq. (2), the points of variable $i$ are the
Chebyshev--Lobatto points
$$
x_{i, j} = \frac{p_i + q_i}{2} + \frac{q_i - p_i}{2} \cos \left( \frac{j \pi}{N_i} \right) ,
\qquad j = 0, \dots, N_i , \qquad N_i \equiv 2^{l_i} ,
\tag{4}
$$
where the level $l_i$ fixes the number $N_i + 1$ of points. The function $F$ is evaluated
on the grid formed by the tensor product of the points of all variables. A type-I discrete
cosine transform along each variable gives the coefficients of Eq. (3) with
$K_i = N_i + 1$, normalized in each variable as in
[Spectral Methods](spectral.qmd#computing-the-coefficients). The level of each variable
starts at its `level_min`. The points of level $l_i$ are a subset of the points of level
$l_i + 1$. Raising the level of variable $i$ by one therefore keeps every value of $F$
already computed, and $F$ is evaluated only at the
$2^{l_i} \prod_{k \ne i} (N_k + 1)$ new grid points, where $l_i$ is the level before the
increase.

The function $F$ is supplied to the construction as a callback of type
[[numcosmo-math|NcmSpectralTensorF]]. Each call receives one array of points per variable,
and $F$ is evaluated at every point of their tensor product. The values are stored with
the last variable running fastest. A part of $F$ that depends on one variable only can
therefore be computed once per point of that variable, instead of once per grid point.

## The Test

A node becomes a panel node when its series passes the test of this section, and is
refined otherwise ([Refinement](#refinement)). The test is on the change of the
coefficients when the grid of one variable is replaced by the grid of the level below,
which keeps every other point. This change needs no new evaluation of $F$.

The $\ell_1$ norm of the coefficients at a fixed index $k$ of variable $i$ is
$$
b_i^k \equiv \sum_{k_{i'} , \, i' \ne i} \left| c^{k_0 \dots k_{n - 1}} \right|_{k_i = k} ,
$$
where the sum runs over the indices of every variable other than $i$. The coefficients of
the grid of level $l_i - 1$ in variable $i$ are those of Eq. (3) folded in $k_i$, as in
[Spectral Methods](spectral.qmd#adaptive-refinement). The $\ell_1$ change of the
coefficients between the two grids is therefore exactly
$$
D_i \equiv 2 \sum_{k > N_i / 2} b_i^k .
\tag{5}
$$
The series of the node passes the test when
$$
D \equiv \sum_{i = 0}^{n - 1} D_i \le \varepsilon \equiv \max \left( \varepsilon_\mathrm{rel} V, \; \varepsilon_\mathrm{abs} \right) ,
\tag{6}
$$
where $V$ is the largest $|F|$ on the current grid of the node, $\varepsilon_\mathrm{rel}$
is the relative tolerance, and $\varepsilon_\mathrm{abs}$ is the absolute tolerance, in
the units of $F$. Both tolerances must be non-negative, and at least one must be positive;
otherwise the construction aborts with an error.

Since $|T_k| \le 1$ on $[-1, 1]$, $D_i$ bounds the largest change of the series on the
node when the grid of variable $i$ is replaced by the grid of the level below. The sum $D$
is the estimate of the error of the series. It is the change between two grids, not the
distance to $F$, and it is not a bound on that distance. A peak of $F$ narrower than the
spacing of the grid and located between two points is absent from the values of $F$ on
the grid. The coefficients are then those of $F$ without the peak, and the series can
pass the test without representing it. When the position and the width of such a peak
are known, the domain is split there before the construction.

## Refinement

A node whose series fails the test of Eq. (6) is refined in one variable $i$. The
variable $i$ has the largest $D_i$ among the variables whose `level_min` is below their
`level_cap`, and is the first of them when several have the same $D_i$. The node is
either split in variable $i$ or its level $l_i$ is raised by one.

- When $l_i$ equals the `level_cap` of variable $i$, the node is split.
- When $l_i$ is one below the `level_cap` and the value of $D_i$ predicted for level
  $l_i + 1$ is above $\varepsilon$, the node is split. The prediction is that of
  [Spectral Methods](spectral.qmd#batch-expansions), applied to $b_i^k$.
- Otherwise the level $l_i$ is raised by one, and the test is repeated.

The split is a bisection, with the single interior edge $(p_i + q_i) / 2$. The two
children are then expanded one after the other, each starting from the `level_min` of
every variable. A split is not made when the node is already `max-depth` bisections below
the node that was empty when the construction started, or when the midpoint is not
strictly inside $[p_i, q_i]$ in floating point. The construction then stops with the
error `NCM_SPECTRAL_TENSOR_BUILDER_ERROR_MAX_DEPTH`, and the table is reset to its domain
and an empty root.

The tolerance $\varepsilon$ must be above the error of the values of $F$. Each coefficient
of Eq. (3) carries the error of those values, which is at least their rounding, of order
$10^{-16} |F|$, and $D$ sums the absolute values of many coefficients. A node whose
$\varepsilon$ is below the value of $D$ produced by that error does not pass the test at
any level, and its bisections end in the error above. The construction may evaluate $F$
many times before that error. For a function of large $|F|$, the absolute tolerance
reaches this limit first. With $|F|$ of order $10^4$, the tolerance
$\varepsilon_\mathrm{abs} = 10^{-12}$ is below the rounding of the values and the
construction fails, while $\varepsilon_\mathrm{rel} = 10^{-12}$ gives
$\varepsilon = 10^{-12} V$ on each node and the construction ends.

A variable whose `level_min` equals its `level_cap` has a fixed number of points,
$2^{l_i} + 1$. It is never chosen for refinement, but its $D_i$ is part of $D$ in
Eq. (6). The node is then refined only in the other variables, and at least one variable
must have its `level_min` below its `level_cap`. When splits in the other variables do
not bring $D$ below $\varepsilon$, the construction stops with the error above.

## Stored Coefficients

A node whose series passes the test becomes a panel node. By default the panel stores all
the coefficients, $K_i = N_i + 1$. With the property `trim-frac` $f > 0$, the panel stores
a leading block of $K_0 \times \dots \times K_{n - 1}$ coefficients instead, obtained by
removing slices of highest index one at a time. At each step, the $\ell_1$ norm of the
slice $k_i = K_i - 1$ of the current block is computed for every variable with $K_i > 1$.
The slice with the smallest norm is removed, that of the first variable when several have
the same norm. The removal continues while
$$
S \le f \varepsilon ,
\tag{7}
$$
where $S$ is the $\ell_1$ norm of all the coefficients removed and $f \in [0, 1)$, and
stops at the first slice that would violate Eq. (7). Since $|T_k| \le 1$, the stored
series differs from the full series by at most $S$ at every point of the panel. The
estimated error of the stored series is therefore at most
$D + S \le (1 + f) \varepsilon$. The number of operations of an evaluation is
proportional to the number of stored coefficients ([Evaluation](#evaluation)), so the
removal reduces it. The removal is greedy, and the block it stores need not be the
smallest that satisfies Eq. (7).

## Continuity between Panels

Each panel is expanded on its own grid, and the series of two panels that share a
boundary are not constrained to agree on it. If the error of each series is at most
$\varepsilon$, the two series differ by at most $2 \varepsilon$ at a point of the
boundary. The table is then continuous across panel boundaries up to $2 \varepsilon$.
This holds only as far as $D$ estimates the error, since $D$ is not a bound
([The Test](#the-test)). Inside a panel, the derivatives of the table are those of one
series. Across a boundary, the derivatives of the two series are not related. A
difference quotient of the table between two points a distance $h$ apart has an error of
up to $2 \varepsilon / h$. Between two points of one panel, the error of the table is one
smooth function, and the error of the quotient tends to its derivative as $h \to 0$.
Between two points on opposite sides of a boundary, the error of the table can jump at
the boundary, and the error of the quotient can grow as $2 \varepsilon / h$ when
$h \to 0$.

The adaptive partition of unity of @Aiton2018 also bisects subdomains at the midpoint, in
every variable that its algorithm marks as unfinished, so a subdomain may be split in
several variables at once. Its neighboring subdomains overlap. Their polynomials are
combined with weights built from infinitely differentiable bump functions of compact
support, normalized to sum to one, and the approximation is infinitely differentiable
across subdomain boundaries. The table described here splits one variable per split and
has no overlap and no weights.

## Symbols and the Code

| Symbol | Code |
|---|---|
| $n$ | `NcmSpectralTensor:n-vars` |
| $a_i$, $b_i$ | arguments `lower`, `upper` of `ncm_spectral_tensor_set_domain`; the bounds of node 0 |
| interior edges $e_1, \dots, e_{m - 1}$ of a split node | argument `edges` of `ncm_spectral_tensor_split`; `edges` of the table, at `edges_offset` of the node |
| $m$, the number of children of a split node | `n_edges` of the node, plus one |
| $p_i$, $q_i$ | `node_bounds` of the table: the lower ends of a node, then its upper ends |
| $K_i$ | argument `n_coeffs` of `ncm_spectral_tensor_set_panel` |
| $c^{k_0 \dots k_{n - 1}}$ | argument `coeffs` of `ncm_spectral_tensor_set_panel`; `work->coeffs` during a build |
| $s_i$ | `s[i]` in `ncm_spectral_tensor_eval_on` |
| $u^{k_1 \dots k_{n - 1}}$ | `d0`, ..., `d3` and `d` in `_ncm_spectral_tensor_basis_2` |
| $T_k (s_i)$ | `T0`, ..., `T3` in `_ncm_spectral_tensor_eval_on_basis`, from `_ncm_spectral_tensor_cheb_T_prod`, `_ncm_spectral_tensor_cheb_T_chains` and `_ncm_spectral_tensor_cheb_T` |
| $l_i$, $N_i$ | `l[i]` and `1u << l[i]` in `_ncm_spectral_tensor_builder_expand` |
| $x_{i, 0}, \dots, x_{i, N_i}$ | the array `work->nodes[i]`, in the order of $j$, filled by `_ncm_spectral_tensor_builder_nodes` |
| refined variable $i$ in [Refinement](#refinement) | `j` in `_ncm_spectral_tensor_builder_expand` |
| $b_i^k$ | `work->b[i]`, from `_ncm_spectral_tensor_builder_coeffs` |
| $D_i$, $D$ | `Di[i]` and the value returned by `_ncm_spectral_tensor_builder_change` |
| $V$ | value returned by `_ncm_spectral_tensor_builder_coeffs` |
| $\varepsilon_\mathrm{rel}$, $\varepsilon_\mathrm{abs}$ | arguments `reltol`, `abstol` of `ncm_spectral_tensor_builder_build` |
| $\varepsilon$ | `tol` in `_ncm_spectral_tensor_builder_expand` |
| $f$ | `NcmSpectralTensorBuilder:trim-frac` |
| $S$, $f \varepsilon$ | `S` and `budget` in `_ncm_spectral_tensor_builder_set_panel` |

## API Reference

The class [[numcosmo-math|NcmSpectralTensor]] implements the table, and the class
[[numcosmo-math|NcmSpectralTensorBuilder]] implements its construction. Their pages list
every function. The operations described on this page are implemented by the following
functions.

- Filling the table: [[numcosmo-math|ncm_spectral_tensor_set_domain]],
  [[numcosmo-math|ncm_spectral_tensor_split]],
  [[numcosmo-math|ncm_spectral_tensor_split_empty]] and
  [[numcosmo-math|ncm_spectral_tensor_set_panel]].
- Evaluating the table: [[numcosmo-math|ncm_spectral_tensor_find_panel]],
  [[numcosmo-math|ncm_spectral_tensor_eval]],
  [[numcosmo-math|ncm_spectral_tensor_eval_on]] and
